x: A chess tactic is a short, usually forcing sequence of moves that wins material or delivers checkmate by exploiting a concrete weakness in the opponent's position. Tactics rest on a handful of patterns that come up again and again: the fork, the pin, the skewer, the discovered attack, deflection and the back-rank mate. Once you learn to recognise them, you start winning pieces and games that used to slip away. Tactics vs strategy Strategy answers the question "what do I want to do in this position?": improve a piece, attack a weak pawn, open a file. Tactics answer "what can I win right now?".

The Philidor position is the model draw: the weaker side holds by keeping its rook on its third rank , so the enemy king cannot advance, and then checking from behind. x: Calculating in chess means predicting a sequence of moves in your head — a variation — and evaluating the position it leads to, without touching the pieces. Strong players follow a four-step method: list the candidate moves , starting with the forcing ones ( checks, captures and threats ); calculate each candidate until the position is quiet; evaluate that position; and only then compare and choose.
